You use the trapassato prossimo (avevo finito, era già partito) to tell what had happened BEFORE another past action, with dopo che, già, appena, non ancora, mai.
I had never seen a painting like that.

Someone had already restored it in 1972.
To form the trapassato prossimo: imperfect of AVERE / ESSERE + participle.
To choose the auxiliary as in the passato prossimo: avevo mangiato, ero partita.
To order two past actions: first (trapassato), then (passato prossimo).
To use dopo che, quando, perché + trapassato.
To use già, appena, non… ancora, non… mai with the trapassato.
To tell the story of a discovery and its history.
An October evening. Matei walks into the trattoria and finds Pietro jumping on the chairs for joy.
Matei! Matei! Mum and Dad are coming to live in Florence!
Really? What fantastic news! When did you find out?
Today! They told me on the phone. But you already knew, didn't you? You've got the face of someone who knew.
Er… Your father had talked to me about it in July. But he had asked me not to tell you.
I knew it! And Grandma? Did Grandma know too?
Me? I had worked it out before anyone. On your birthday your mother had already looked up Florence schools on the internet.
And why didn't they tell you straight away?
Because they hadn't found work here yet. They didn't want to give him false hope.
But now Dad has found a job in a hospital and Mum in a school. They had even found the house before they called me!
On via Maggio! A hundred metres from the trattoria! So I can come to Grandma's every day.
(smiles) Every day… Let's hope he does his homework too, now and then.
Matei, my wish came true! I told you the candles work!

The imperfect of AVERE: a-VE-vo, a-ve-VA-mo, a-VE-va-no. Watch the moving stress.
E-ro, e-ra-VA-mo, E-ra-no. A single, lightly rolled R.
Double LL and stress on "FI": cal-li-gra-FEE-a.
Trapassato prossimo = imperfect of AVERE or ESSERE + participle. The auxiliary is chosen exactly as in the passato prossimo, and with ESSERE the participle agrees.
It corresponds to the English past perfect and the Romanian mai-mult-ca-perfect: "terminasem", "plecasem". But in Italian it's used much more than in Romanian!
The trapassato shows an action completed BEFORE another past action. Think of a timeline:
e noi siamo arrivati alle sette.

In spoken Romanian we often use the perfect compus for both: "Când am ajuns, trenul a plecat" — but that would mean it left AFTER you arrived! In Italian the difference is compulsory: "era partito" = it had already left.
3. With già, appena, non ancora, mai
The adverbs go between the auxiliary and the participle:
Non ero mai stata a Sibiu.
I had never been to Sibiu.
After they had found work, they looked for a house.
I didn't call you because I had lost my phone.
When I opened the crate, someone had already opened it.
With the pronouns lo / la, the participle agrees here too: "La lettera? L'avevo già letta."
The trapassato often appears when we report what someone said about the past:
"I've found a house." → He said he had found a house.
"I've been to Naples." → She said she had been to Naples.

Before leaving for Sibiu, Matei had to finish one last job: the small fifteenth-century Madonna he had been working on for a year. Ilinca had seen it in February, Bellini had checked it every week, and now only the back was left.

One Tuesday in November, Matei removed the old protective canvas covering the back of the painting. Underneath, stuck to the wood with a little glue, was a yellow envelope. Someone had hidden it there many years before.
Matei called Giulia. Together they opened the envelope with tweezers, very slowly, the way you open an old painting. Inside was a handwritten sheet, in small, precise handwriting.

"Florence, March 1972. This Madonna was in the church of San Frediano when the water came, on the 4th of November 1966. The mud had covered her up to the eyes. For six years she stayed in a storeroom with hundreds of wounded paintings. When I found her, I thought she was lost for ever.
I cleaned her for four months, every evening, with my six-year-old grandson beside me. He had never seen a restoration. I had given him a tiny brush and told him only: Look. And don't touch anything.
Whoever finds this letter, in fifty or a hundred years, will be a restorer like me. I ask only one thing: treat this Madonna like a daughter. She has suffered enough already. — Ernesto Bellini"
Matei and Giulia looked at each other in silence. Bellini. The professor's grandfather. The six-year-old grandson with the tiny brush was him, the professor, as a child.

Matei remembered what the professor had said to Ilinca in February: "Your brother treats her like a daughter." Back then he had thought it was just a kind remark. Now he understood: Bellini had always known where that Madonna came from. But he had never seen the letter.

Giulia, on the other hand, had already understood everything. "Remember? At the Christmas dinner he had told us about his grandfather, the brush, the Sundays at the Uffizi. But he had never mentioned this Madonna. Maybe he didn't know it was her."
They went to his office together. Bellini took the sheet and read it once, slowly. Then he read it again. His hands, which had never trembled in front of a masterpiece, were trembling.

"I didn't know," he said at last, in a voice they had never heard from him. "My grandfather had never told me. I remember the evenings, the mud, the smell… But I didn't know he had left a letter. For me. For whoever would come after."

Then he opened his desk drawer and took out a worn, tiny brush. "Here. It's the same one. I've been using it for over forty years." He put it in Matei's hand. "Now it's yours. Take it to Sibiu. And one day give it to whoever comes after you."

Matei didn't know what to say. Giulia, however, said what everyone was thinking: "Professor, your grandfather would be proud of you." And Bellini, for the first time since they'd known him, smiled with tears in his eyes.
